title: Off-policy Monte Carlo and Importance Sampling
oneLiner: How to learn about one strategy from data produced by a different strategy, by reweighting what happened, and why the reweighting can go badly wrong.

what.html:
Off-policy learning means the data comes from one strategy (the behaviour policy) but you want to know how well another strategy (the target policy) would do. You can't rerun the past, so you reweight each recorded episode: episodes the target would have been likely to produce count more; ones it would never produce count zero.

Everyday versionJudging a new treatment protocol from old hospital records: the doctors back then decided by their own judgement. Cases where they happened to do what the new protocol says are informative; cases where they did something else tell you nothing about the protocol.

why.html:
• Learn the best (greedy) strategy while still exploring.
  • Evaluate a new policy from logs before risking it in the real world.
  • Understand why reweighting can produce wild estimates, and how to tame them.

how.title: Two policies, two jobs
how.html: The behaviour policy acts and produces data; the target policy is what you're learning about. The behaviour must sometimes take every action the target might take (coverage), or you have no evidence about those actions.

how.title: The reweighting factor
how.html: Multiply, step by step, "how likely the target was to do this" divided by "how likely the behaviour was to do this". Three steps with target odds 0.8, 0.7, 0.8 and behaviour odds 0.5, 0.4, 0.5 give 0.448/0.1 = 4.48. The environment's randomness cancels out, so no model is needed.

how.title: Two ways to average
how.html: Ordinary: add up weight × return and divide by the number of episodes. Weighted: divide by the total weight instead. With returns 4.24, 2.61, 2.33 and weights 6.667, 0.125, 1.5, ordinary gives 10.70 (higher than any return seen!), weighted gives 3.87.

how.title: When averages never settle
how.html: Ordinary reweighting is unbiased on average, but rare episodes with huge weights can make it jump around forever: in one simple example its variance is literally infinite.

how.title: How much data do you really have?
how.html: Effective sample size = (sum of weights)² / sum of squared weights. Three episodes with weights 6.667, 0.125 and 1.5 are worth about 1.5 episodes. Low numbers are a warning sign.

how.title: Update as you go
how.html: Keep a running total weight C. For each new return: C += weight, estimate += (weight/C) × (return − estimate). (2, 5), (1, 2), (3, 4) give 5, then 4, then 4.

how.title: Learning the best policy while exploring
how.html: Walk each episode backwards updating the greedy policy's values; stop at the first step where the explorer did something the greedy policy wouldn't. Only the end of each episode teaches anything, which makes this slow.

demo.html: Press Play. The true answer is 1. The weighted estimate (green) sits at 1 almost immediately; the ordinary estimates keep lurching whenever a rare long streak arrives with a huge weight.

example.html:
Why 10.70 is suspicious. All three observed returns are between 2.33 and 4.24, yet ordinary importance sampling estimates 10.70, because the first episode's weight (6.667) is multiplied by its return and divided only by 3. Weighted importance sampling divides by the total weight 8.29, giving 3.87, a sensible average of what was seen.

Supplementary The same idea of a ratio between new and old policy shows up, with clipping, in PPO.

misunderstandings: Off-policy data needs a model to correct.
The transition probabilities cancel in the ratio.
Ordinary IS is unbiased but can have infinite variance.
It is biased, but the bias vanishes and variance is far lower.
Every step of every episode teaches the greedy policy.
Only the tail after the last non-greedy action does.
takeaways: Behaviour b generates data; target π is learned about; coverage required.
Ratio ρ = Π π/b; dynamics cancel (worked 4.48).
Ordinary IS unbiased but high variance; weighted IS stable (10.70 vs 3.87).
Off-policy MC control breaks at the first non-greedy action.
thirty: Off-policy learning evaluates or improves a target policy π using episodes from a behaviour policy b, provided b covers every action π might take. Returns are reweighted by ρ = Π π(Aₖ|Sₖ)/b(Aₖ|Sₖ), in which the dynamics cancel (worked 0.448/0.1 = 4.48). Ordinary importance sampling divides Σ ρG by the count (unbiased, possibly infinite variance, as in the one-state loop example), weighted importance sampling by Σ ρ (biased but stable); returns (4.24, 2.61, 2.33) with weights (6.667, 0.125, 1.5) give 10.70 vs 3.87. Effective sample size (Σw)²/Σw² (here 1.47) diagnoses weight degeneracy. Weighted estimates update incrementally with C ← C + W, V ← V + (W/C)(G − V). Off-policy MC control walks episodes backwards and stops at the first non-greedy action.
